extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent attorneys, and federal judges
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and principles for who decides the meaning of patent claim terms (judge vs. jury) and how claim terms should be interpreted in litigation. Focuses on allocation of claim-construction questions, the role of expert evidence, and considerations (historical, functional, and policy) informing that allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of patent claims is a question of law for the court
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of a patent, including terms of art within its claim, is exclusively within the province of the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Seventh Amendment does not require a jury to decide the meaning of disputed claim terms; judges should construe claims as a legal determination. The Court expressly affirms that judges — not juries — determine claim meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct allocation: claim construction (law) vs. infringement (fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent litigation has two elements: (1) construing the patent (a question of law for the court) and (2) determining whether infringement occurred (a question of fact for the jury).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts decide the legal scope of claims; juries decide whether the accused product or process falls within that scope. Trial procedure should reflect this division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define scope and must 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim 'particularly poin[t] out and distinctly clai[m] the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention' and 'defin[e] the scope of a patent grant.' Claims cover processes, machines, manufactures, compositions, or designs, not merely functions or scientific explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting or construing claims, focus on their role in delimiting patent rights and informing the public of what is and is not claimed; avoid claiming mere results or abstract functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret claim terms in light of the specification and the patent as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim term must be defined in a way that comports with the instrument as a whole; claim construction requires interpreting the claim in the context of the specification and entire patent document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges should perform a holistic analysis of the patent to ensure internal coherence; isolated dictionary meanings may be inadequate if inconsistent with the specification or claim structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony is admissible to explain technical terms but does not supplant judicial construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical experts may provide evidence (in pais) about the outward embodiment or the meaning of technical terms, yet the court retains ultimate responsibility to construe the patent and is not bound to accept expert characterizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expert evidence to inform the court’s interpretive work (e.g., to explain terms of art or the nature of physical embodiments), but the judge must evaluate whether the expert's proposed definition fits the patent as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate document interpretation from identification of outward embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between construing the meaning of words of a document (a legal task for the court) and identifying or comparing physical embodiments described by patents (a factual task that may be for the jury with expert aid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Bischoff and Tucker illustrate that experts and juries may resolve whether physical objects embody an invention, while interpreting the text of the patent remains a judicial function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical test for Seventh Amendment allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a particular trial issue must be decided by a jury under the Seventh Amendment, compare the modern cause or issue to 18th-century English common-law practice or appropriate analogues and seek the best analogy where no exact antecedent exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First determine whether the cause of action was traditionally at law; if so, analyze whether the specific subsidiary issue was historically a jury matter. Where history is unclear, rely on analogy to known practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where historical antecedent is lacking, use precedent, comparative skills, and statutory policy
rubrics_metrics.description: If historical common-law practice does not resolve whether an issue is for judge or jury, allocate responsibility by consulting existing precedent and assessing (1) comparative interpretive skills of judges and juries and (2) statutory policy considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should weigh legal precedent, the relative ability of decisionmakers to interpret technical documents, and policy needs (e.g., uniformity) to decide allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional consideration: judges are better suited to construe technical patent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Because construction of written instruments is a judicial function and patent claims are often highly technical, judges, by training and discipline, are more likely than juries to give a proper interpretation that preserves internal coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deference to judges reduces the risk of inconsistent or unschooled interpretations; judges are better positioned to assess how expert testimony fits the whole patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity and public notice require judicial claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocating claim construction to courts promotes uniformity and certainty in patent scope, which is necessary for protecting patentees, encouraging inventive activity, and informing the public what is dedicated to the public domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial construction supports stare decisis and inter- and intrajurisdictional consistency (and undergirds the purpose of the Federal Circuit). Jury determinations of claim meaning would undermine that uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims lacked clear 18th-century antecedent; use specification-construction practice as closest analogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Because modern claims did not exist in 18th-century patent practice, the closest antecedent is construction of specifications, and historical reports show judges — not juries — construed specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using historical analogy, treat specification-construction practice as the most relevant antecedent for resolving who should construe modern claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh Amendment protects only incidents fundamental to jury trial; use substance/procedure and law/fact distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Seventh Amendment right to a jury pertains to rights as they existed at common law; only incidents regarded as fundamental to the jury system are beyond legislative allocation. The line is often drawn between issues of law (judge) and issues of fact (jury).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a subsidiary issue must be decided by a jury, analyze whether the issue is a core incident of the 1791 jury right, using historical practice and functional analysis; don’t conflate evidentiary presentation with entitlement to jury determination.
